title: SHINIGAMAE
subtitle: Personal digital workshop
problem: Everything I make lived in five different places, none of which I owned, and none of which talked to each other.
approach: Design the language first in Figma, then build a static Astro shell against it, with a token layer strict enough that the design cannot drift silently. Five sync scripts pull the sources in and commit what they find, so no page waits on someone else's API to render.
result: This site — 480-odd pages off five feeds, a dark ground and a light one, and a drift report that says when code and design have stopped agreeing.
lessons: Publishing styles in Figma matters more than any sync script
A token layer is only real if nothing can bypass it — a second theme then costs one file
A feed you sync and commit beats an API you call at read time
Deciding the shell before the pages saved a rewrite

title: GUILD MANAGEMENT PLATFORM
subtitle: Roster, match records and a Discord bot for a Where Winds Meet guild
role: Solo: architecture, build and operations, for the guild
problem: A guild of about ninety players ran on a Google Sheet that published itself as encrypted files, with the decryption key shipped in the browser bundle, so the private roster was readable by anyone who looked. Events, match footage and player stats lived in three other places on top of that.
approach: Three parts, and one of them owns the data. An Angular site on GitHub Pages and a Discord bot both talk to a .NET 10 Minimal API over Postgres. The bot answers Discord over HTTP instead of holding a gateway connection open. Azure Functions sync live player stats from the game's own gateway, but only write when something has changed. Permissions are checked at the API, never in the client, and every design choice answers to one bill: how many hours the database is awake.
result: Three repositories and about 500 commits in fifteen weeks, all on free-tier hosting. The guild gets Discord sign-in with three nested roles, GvG match history with footage, self-run PvP tournaments, scouting across some 6,500 opponent players, and a Discord bot with 41 commands.

architecture.label: CLIENTS
architecture.link: HTTPS: app JWT from Discord sign-in, or a bot key

architecture.label: DATA
nodes: PostgreSQL on Neon, scales to zero

architecture.label: SYNC
nodes: Azure Functions: timers and on-demand refresh

lessons: A static site cannot keep a secret from its viewers. An encryption key in the bundle is a key handed out.
On a serverless database the bill is hours awake, not queries run, so the cheapest sync is one that never wakes it.
Enforce permissions where the data lives. A role in localStorage is a suggestion anyone can edit.
A green deploy proves the deploy ran, not that anything works: a 200 means the function ran, not that data arrived.
Archive a third-party source while it is still up. The community relay that held our match history stopped resolving overnight, and our archive was the last copy.
Generate the reference from the code. The hand-written command list had gone wrong in three places at once.

title: READING TIMELINE
subtitle: Goodreads without the noise
problem: I wanted the shape of a reading year, not a feed of other people's reviews.
approach: Pull my own shelf data, reduce it to finish dates and a single personal note per book, and render it as one line.
result: A year of reading readable at a glance.
lessons: One sentence per book is more honest than a star rating
Most of the data was not worth keeping
